bull_bear.title: Management quality / tone

bull_bear.body: The INR 460-500 Cr inventory buildup represents blocked revenue of ~INR 1,000 Cr that will flip to top-line immediately upon court order implementation; Retail strategy is a trojan horse to blend own ethanol at higher margins rather than pure trading; SAF plant location (Andhra) strategically chosen for proximity to refineries, airport, and port for export flexibility.
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- MD frames retail expansion as deliberate restraint: "we prioritised disciplined capital allocation, superior locations and sustainable unit economics over rapid network expansion" against Middle East tensions and elevated crude prices.
- Existing 2,000 KLPD ethanol platform at 60.57% utilisation is presented as growth "without significant additional capital expenditure".
- Growth capital is being de-risked through partners and government money: share purchase transactions completed for both the Sumitomo and GAIL JVs, NABARD financing for CBG, Rs 150 crore PM JI-VAN grant and CFA eligibility for SAF/CBG.
- Consolidated ratio analysis as disclosed: ROCE 20.35%, ROE 14.42%, Debt/Equity 0.59, TOL/TNW 1.28, Current Ratio 1.82, ISCR 2.59, DSCR 1.36.
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation policy (investor deck)

bull_bear.body:
- "Largest Ethanol producer in India based on installed capacity" (Company's own Annual Report claim); 2000 KLPD across 5 units described as "India's largest multi-feed & year-round Ethanol platform"
- "India's only dedicated biofuels company, combining agricultural strength with industrial scale to deliver diversified bioenergy solutions"
- "The first biofuels company in the country to attain Oil Marketing Company (OMC) status", enabling end-to-end participation from production to retail
- One of the first producers of CBG under the Government of India's SATAT scheme (introduced 2018)
- Feedstock flexibility: approximately 1,300 KLPD of grain-based dual-feed capacity commissioned in FY2025-26, converting nearly 65% of installed ethanol capacity into a flexible dual-feed platform enabling near year-round operations
- Global partnerships giving capital and technology access: strategic collaborations with Sumitomo Corporation (in TruAlt Gas Private Limited) and GAIL (India) Limited (in Leafiniti Bioenergy Private Limited) for CBG; Honeywell UOP for SAF FEED
- Downstream integration via own retail fuel network — 7 outlets operational, strengthening direct consumer interface
- Logistics adjacency claimed in the Corporate Overview: 4 major international airports and 5 major ports near the asset base
- Early mover positioning in Sustainable Aviation Fuel, "positioned to establish one of the largest SAF facilities in the country"
- Diversified lender panel: State Bank of India, IREDA, Indian Overseas Bank, Canara Bank, Federal Bank, Yes Bank, Kotak Mahindra Bank
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Dependence on Oil Marketing Company offtake — OMCs sharply cut lifting despite the Company being production-ready — The Board's Report states revenue 'was significantly impacted due to a sharp reduction in lifting by OMCs despite operational readiness and available production capacities'. This is a demand-side concentration risk the Company does not control: capacity and readiness were not the constraint, the buyer's lifting decision was. It is the single largest stated cause of the year's revenue shortfall.
- Unexecuted ethanol allocation contingent on a court order — the pending 15 crore litre allocation following the Hon'ble Karnataka High Court order — The Board's Report attributes part of the revenue impact to 'delays in implementation and execution relating to the pending 15 crore litre allocation following the Hon'ble Karnataka High Court order'. Volumes the Company is counting on for recovery sit behind judicial and administrative execution rather than commercial demand, and the timing of realisation is outside management's control.
- Rising finance costs and leverage from the growth build-out — The Board's Report states the fall in profit after tax was 'primarily attributable to an increase in finance costs arising from additional working capital facilities availed by the Company to support its business operations and also interest incurred on the account of grain-based plant established during the year', compounded by higher depreciation from capitalising the grain-based plant. Structurally: a capital-intensive expansion is being funded with debt while offtake is being withheld — the two risks compound. Credit standing is CRISIL A-/Stable (reaffirmed October 28, 2025) with India Ratings assigning IND A-/Stable / IND A2+ on bank loan facilities in April 2026.
- Governance compliance failure — no Woman Independent Director on the Board through the reporting period — A Secretarial Audit Report observation records that 'The Company failed to appoint the Woman Independent Director in compliance Regulation No. 17(1)a of SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015.' Management responds that the matter is receiving the highest priority and that it is in the advanced stage of finalizing a candidate, but the breach ran the full year in the Company's first year as a listed entity.
- Data privacy and cybersecurity — Listed by the Company as material issue 2 and classified as a pure Risk with NEGATIVE financial implications. Mitigation stated as advanced IT security systems, periodic vulnerability assessments and data encryption protocols. Relevant for an entity that has just become a listed, multi-site industrial operator with JV partners.
- Climate strategy and energy/emissions management — Material issues 4 and 5. Energy and Emissions Management is flagged as both Risk and Opportunity (positive and negative implications); Climate Strategy is flagged as a pure Risk with negative implications. For a biofuels producer this cuts both ways — the decarbonisation mandate is the demand driver, but the Company's own process emissions, feedstock footprint and carbon-intensity validation determine whether its product qualifies under tightening low-carbon fuel standards.
- Human rights exposure with the governing policy not yet in place — Material issue 12, a pure Risk with negative implications. The mitigation column concedes the Company 'is actively in the process of implementing a comprehensive Human Rights Policy' — i.e. the policy does not yet exist. The risks it names explicitly are forced labour, discrimination and unsafe working conditions, which is a live exposure given the Company's stated use of independent contractors overseeing on-site contract labour.
- Employee health and safety across multi-site industrial and construction operations — Material issue 13, a pure Risk with negative implications. The Company runs five distilleries plus five CBG plants under construction and a growing retail network; the Board's Report notes regular safety inspections and audits at 'all plants and project sites'. Construction-phase exposure is at its peak in FY27 with four CBG plants due for commissioning.
- Sustainable value chain and supplier dependence — Material issue 14, flagged as both Risk and Opportunity with positive and negative implications. The mitigation text speaks of 'building a reliable and responsible supply chain' and strengthening supplier relationships. Feedstock — sugarcane derivatives and grain — is the Company's dominant cost and its availability, pricing and sustainability credentials are set outside the Company.
- Labour management and industrial relations — Material issue 10, flagged as Risk and Opportunity with positive and negative implications. The Board's Report claims operations 'have been free from major work stoppages due to labour disputes or work cessation' and that attrition reflects stable retention, but no attrition figure is given in this routed text and the workforce includes contract labour engaged through independent contractors.

business.title: Challenges → beneficiaries & losers

business.body:
- Described as the "Largest Ethanol producer in India based on installed capacity" and "One of India's largest biofuels players", combining "agricultural strength with industrial scale to deliver diversified bioenergy solutions".
- Claims to be "The first biofuels company in the country to attain Oil Marketing Company (OMC) status", and "One of the first producers of CBG under the Sustainable Alternative Towards Affordable Transportation (SATAT) scheme introduced by the Government of India in 2018".
- Positioned as "one of the early movers in Sustainable Aviation Fuel projects, positioned to establish one of the largest SAF facilities in the country".
- Institutional partnerships are presented as the moat in green gas: JV with Sumitomo Corporation (4 CBG plants under TruAlt Gas Pvt. Ltd.) and with Maharatna PSU GAIL (India) Limited (6 CBG projects via Leafiniti Bioenergy).
business.title: Positioning (investor deck)

business.body:
- [Sector policy] The deck flags an evolving procurement backdrop: "disruptions witnessed during ESY 2025-26 resulted in lower-than-anticipated allocations and temporary underutilisation of industry capacities", while India achieved "20% ethanol blending five years ahead of schedule" with capacity "approaching 2,000 crore litres per annum".
- [Regulation - CBG] "The CBG Blending Obligation (CBO) mandates City Gas Distribution (CGD) entities to blend CBG into CNG (transport) and PNG (domestic) segments, commencing at 1% in FY 2025-26 and progressively"; Union Budget 2026-27 exempted central excise duty on the biogas/CBG component in blended CNG, correcting "structural double taxation".
- [Blending roadmap] Introduction of "E22, E25, E27 and E30 BIS standards alongside future flex-fuel vehicle ecosystems" is cited as the long-term ethanol demand pathway; sectoral events to watch include a dedicated CBG policy framework that "could unlock a ~USD 30 billion investment opportunity" and notification of India's SAF policy framework.
- [Listing status] Q1 FY27 is described as "our first year-on-year first quarter performance as a listed company".
business.title: Notable from the deck

business.body: TruAlt Bioenergy is a renewable energy company engaged in the manufacturing and sale of ethanol and allied bioenergy products, having commenced commercial operations in FY2022-23 and listed in October 2025. It operates five 1G ethanol distilleries in Karnataka on a multi-feed, year-round platform, produces Extra Neutral Alcohol, CO2 and fermented organic manure, and is building a Compressed Biogas business through two subsidiaries with strategic partners, alongside a downstream biofuel retail network. Customers span oil and gas companies, government agencies and state-owned enterprises, spirits producers and major consumer-goods companies; the entity reports NIL exports as a percentage of turnover.
business.title: What they do

business.body:
- **Current products:** Compressed Biogas (CBG), First-Generation (1G) Ethanol, Extra Neutral Alcohol (ENA), Fermented Organic Manure, CO2, Biofuel Dispensing Stations, Motor Spirit (MS) & HSD (High-Speed Diesel)
- **Proposed products:** Liquid Fermented Organic Manure (LFOM), Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF), Future Fuels & High Value By-Products, Dried Distillers Grains with Solubles (DDGS), Second-Generation (2G) Ethanol, Mevalonolactone / Mevalonic Acid
business.title: Products & brands

business.body:
- Leafiniti Bioenergy Private Limited — subsidiary: 51% held by the listed entity (BRSR Section A item 23). CIN U11202KA2020PTC196716. Subsidiary since September 18, 2023, under Section 2(87)(ii). Operates the Company's Compressed Bio-Gas business alongside GAIL (India) Limited — the AOC-1 note records a strategic collaboration with 'GAIL India Limited in Leafiniti Bioenergy Private Limited for the development and implementation of Compressed Bio-Gas (CBG) projects in identified location'. Runs CBG Unit 1 at Jamkhandi (operational) and the six identified CBG Units 6-11. Does NOT participate in the listed entity's Business Responsibility initiatives. A footnote states it 'ceased to be the wholly owned subsidiary of the Company w.e.f. March 18, 2026' — i.e. a dilution from wholly-owned to 51%, not an exit. Also a counterparty under AOC-2 for a sub-lease of office space, a master supply agreement for sale of diesel and steam, transaction-based support-service arrangements, and interest income on a loan repayable on demand.
- TruAlt Gas Private Limited — subsidiary: 51% held by the listed entity (BRSR Section A item 23). CIN U35201KA2024PTC192874. Subsidiary since October 27, 2025, under Section 2(87)(ii). Named in Form AOC-1 Part A as the one subsidiary 'yet to commence operations'. The AOC-1 note records a strategic collaboration with Sumitomo Corporation in TruAlt Gas Private Limited for development and implementation of CBG projects. Holds CBG Units 2-5 (Mudhol, Kerakalmatti, Badami, Daund) all in construction. Does NOT participate in the listed entity's Business Responsibility initiatives. Also an AOC-2 counterparty for a sale of land and a sub-lease of office space (11 months, renewable annually).
- Nirani Sugars Limited — related party: CIN U15424KA2020PLC142790. Described in Form AOC-2 as 'Common Directors or Company in which Directors have [interest]'. Two arm's-length arrangements: (i) a Master Supply Agreement running April 01, 2025 to March 31 [year truncated] covering sale of steam and chemicals BY the Company and purchase of raw materials BY the Company; and (ii) a Lease Agreement, ongoing subject to annual renewal, for the registered office, corporate offices and other premises. Board approval dated May 13 [year truncated]. This is the Company's single largest related-party counterparty by nature of dealing — it sits on BOTH sides of the trade (raw-material supplier and steam/chemicals customer).
- Riga Sugars Co Ltd — related party: Listed company in which Mr. Vijaykumar Murugesh Nirani (Managing Director) and Mr. Vishal Nirani (Executive Director) both hold directorships as at March 31, 2026. Disclosed under 'other listed entities where the Directors are holding directorship', not in the AOC-1 or AOC-2 tables.
- 63 Moons Technologies Limited — related party: Listed entity in which Mr. Chandrasekhar Kanekal, Independent Director, holds a directorship as at March 31, 2026. Disclosed under 'other listed entities where the Directors are holding directorship' only; no transactional relationship with the Company is stated.
- Associates / Joint Ventures — associate: STATED ABSENCE, not silence. Form AOC-1 Part B ('Associates and Joint Ventures') is filled in as 'Not Applicable' throughout, and item 4 'Number of Associate / Joint Venture' carries no entity. The Company therefore has NO associates and NO joint ventures under Section 129(3) as at March 31, 2026. Note the tension with the MD's message, which calls Leafiniti and TruAlt Gas 'our strategic joint ventures' — legally both are consolidated 51% subsidiaries, not JVs.

outlook.body:
- Support the Government of India's ethanol blending programme and the transition to greener energy, while continuously enhancing production capabilities and optimising resource utilisation — the Company states it did not undergo any change in the nature of its business during FY2025-26.
- Expand beyond ethanol into compressed biogas (CBG) and Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) — the routed text frames India's own policy direction as 'expanding its focus beyond ethanol towards compressed biogas (CBG), biodiesel and Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF)', which is the market the Company positions against.
- Strengthen corporate governance as a listed entity: cure the flagged non-compliance by appointing a Woman Independent Director, and place secretarial audit on a five-year footing (Mr. Deepak Sadhu recommended as Secretarial Auditor for FY2026-27 to FY2030-31).
- Maintain an independent internal-audit function — M/s. ZADN & Associates, Chartered Accountants, Mumbai appointed as Internal Auditors for FY2025-26, with the Audit Committee monitoring implementation of audit recommendations including those strengthening risk management policies and systems.
- Maintain an agile, high-performance and diverse workplace with harmonious industrial relations across facilities; the Company reports operations free from major work stoppages due to labour disputes.
- Retain and reinvest, with no cash returned to shareholders. The Board has not recommended any dividend for FY2025-26, stating that 'Considering the capital-intensive nature of the business, the business growth plan of the Company and with a view to plough back profits, your Board has not recommended any dividend ... to build a strong base for long-term sustainable growth.' A formal Dividend Distribution Policy under Regulation 43A of SEBI LODR was formulated and approved at the Board meeting of March 21, 2024, setting out the parameters and circumstances the Board will weigh when determining distributions; it is published on the Company's website. No amount was transferred to the General Reserve during the year. The Company has not issued any convertible instruments. On executive pay, the AGM notice seeks approval to fix remuneration by way of commission to Mr. Vishal Nirani, Executive Director, effective April 1, 2026, with an explicit clawback of the commission in any year of loss or inadequacy of profits, and Board discretion to modify terms within the member-approved limit. The AGM also seeks ratification of Cost Auditors' remuneration for FY ending March 31, 2027. Governance intent is stated in the Corporate Governance philosophy section as ethical business practices, integrity, accountability and compliance, with Board committees constituted for audit, risk management, nomination and remuneration, and stakeholder relationships.
- Human Rights Policy is being implemented but does NOT yet exist — 'Company is actively in the process of implementing a comprehensive Human Rights Policy, meticulously aligned with globally recognized frameworks and standards', to be supported by regular audits, grievance redressal mechanisms and employee awareness initiatives addressing forced labour, discrimination and unsafe working conditions. This is the only concrete, trackable forward ESG commitment in the routed BRSR material-issues table.
- Fourteen material responsible business conduct issues formally identified and each classified as Risk / Opportunity / both with a stated direction of financial implication: Corporate Governance (both), Data Privacy & Cybersecurity (risk), Risk Management (risk), Energy & Emissions Management (both), Climate Strategy (risk), Water Management (opportunity), Waste Management (opportunity), Product Sustainability (opportunity), Human Capital Development (opportunity), Labour Management (both), Diversity Equity & Inclusion (opportunity), Human Rights (risk), Employee Health & Safety (risk), Sustainable Value Chain (both).
- SIX of the fourteen material issues carry a BLANK mitigation column, printed as '-': Water Management, Waste Management, Product Sustainability, Human Capital Development, Diversity Equity & Inclusion, and Labour Management. Under the stated convention a printed '-' is a stated nil, so the Company has declared NO adaptation or mitigation approach for these six. Note that five of the six are classified 'Opportunity' (where a mitigation approach is arguably not required), but Labour Management is classified 'Risk and Opportunity' and still carries no mitigation — that is a genuine gap, not a formatting artefact.
- POSH: an Internal Committee is constituted with four (4) members, all of whom are women. Nil complaints of sexual harassment received, nil disposed and nil pending beyond ninety days during FY2025-26. A Policy for Prevention of Sexual Harassment has been adopted and periodic awareness sessions conducted.
- Compliance with the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 confirmed, including maternity leave, nursing breaks and other prescribed benefits.
- Occupational health and safety: the Company states it adheres to Occupational Health and Safety management standards with regular safety inspections and audits at all plants and project sites, and health/safety awareness programmes across locations. No certification (e.g. ISO 45001), no injury-rate metric and no safety target is stated in this routed text.
- Grievance redressal GAPS disclosed: Customers and Value Chain Partners both answer 'No' to having a grievance redressal mechanism in place, with the Company stating the mechanism is instead embedded in its contracts so 'no separate policy has been formulated in this regard'. Nil complaints recorded from either group in FY2025-26 and FY2024-25.
- Internal control and risk oversight: M/s. ZADN & Associates, Chartered Accountants, Mumbai appointed as Internal Auditors for FY2025-26; the Audit Committee reviews the adequacy and effectiveness of the internal control environment and monitors implementation of audit recommendations 'including those relating to strengthening the Company's risk management policies and systems'.
- The Company states it adheres to BRSR requirements reporting against the National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct principles.
- NO quantified ESG target of any kind appears in this routed text — no emissions-reduction target, no renewable-energy share, no water-intensity, waste, diversity or safety target, and no target year. Every material-issue entry is qualitative narrative. This is an honest absence, not an extraction gap.

outlook.body: TruAlt's expansion runs on four tracks. (1) Ethanol: the installed base is five 1G distilleries in Karnataka aggregating 2000 KLPD, described as 'India's largest multi-feed & year-round Ethanol platform', of which 1300 KLPD is dual feed — Jamkhandi 500 KLPD (Dual Feed Integration 450 KLPD), Mudhol 700 KLPD (Dual Feed 550 KLPD), Khanapur 400 KLPD, Kerakalmatti 200 KLPD (Dual Feed 300 KLPD) and Badami 200 KLPD. The Board's Report records capitalisation of a grain-based plant to the extent of 1300 KLPD during the year. (2) Compressed BioGas: a six-plant build-out plus a further six identified. CBG Unit 1 at Jamkhandi (10.20 TPD, Leafiniti Bioenergy) is Operational; Unit 2 Mudhol (20.00 TPD) is in construction and expected operational by end of Q2 FY27; Unit 3 Kerakalmatti (20.00 TPD) and Unit 4 Badami (20.00 TPD) by end of Q3 FY27; Unit 5 Daund, Maharashtra (20.00 TPD) by end of Q4 FY27 — Units 2 to 5 sit in TruAlt Gas Pvt. Ltd. Units 6 to 11 (72.00 TPD aggregate) are with Leafiniti Bioenergy at locations identified in Karnataka & Maharashtra, where 'Lands for six units have been jointly identified.' Total CBG portfolio capacity is stated at 162.2 TPD, of which only 10.20 TPD is operational today. (3) SAF: a proposed 100 million litres/annum Sustainable Aviation Fuel plant. (4) Retail: 7 biofuel outlets operational with 4 more under construction, taking the network to 11 across Karnataka under Phase 1 of a stated 100-outlet rollout. On the rupee side, the only quantum stated is the capital-commitments named disclosure (contracts remaining to be executed on capital account, net of advances). Notably, the BRSR Principle 2 leadership table prints '-' for both R&D and Capex investments in technologies improving environmental and social impacts — a stated nil, not a blank.

outlook.body:
- Global biofuels are described as shifting from a climate-driven policy initiative into 'a strategic pillar of energy security, industrial competitiveness and sustainable economic growth', with governments treating them as a means to cut imported-crude dependence, strengthen domestic supply chains and enhance farmer incomes.
- Global biofuel production reached a record 192 billion litres in 2024 — approximately 121 billion litres of ethanol, 50 billion litres of biodiesel, 20 billion litres of renewable diesel (HVO) and 1.44 billion litres of SAF.
- The IEA projects global biofuel demand to increase to approximately 238 billion litres by 2030 in its main case, with stronger policy support potentially driving demand to 310 billion litres.
- Per IEA Renewables 2025, renewable energy consumption in transport is expected to increase by 50% by 2030 with liquid biofuels accounting for approximately 35% of that growth; the IEA has revised its global biofuel demand forecast upwards by 50% versus previous projections.
- Biofuel demand in India alone is expected to increase by around 80% by 2030, making it one of the fastest-growing biofuel markets globally.
- Ethanol remains the dominant biofuel at nearly two-thirds of global production; renewable diesel and SAF are the fastest-growing segments, driven by heavy transport and aviation.
- SAF is anticipated to be the fastest-growing segment of the renewable fuels market — IEA projects global SAF consumption rising from approximately 1 billion litres in 2024 to around 9 billion litres by 2030, supported by aviation blending mandates and incentive mechanisms.
- Biofuels today contribute nearly 90% of all renewable energy consumed in the transport sector, letting decarbonisation happen on existing fuel infrastructure.
- Per the OECD-FAO Agricultural Outlook, global biofuel demand is projected to grow steadily through 2034, supported by higher blending mandates, expanding transport fuel demand and increasing investment in advanced biofuels and SAF; countries with abundant agricultural resources, strong policy frameworks and integrated value chains are expected to lead.
- IEA expects bioenergy to account for approximately 95% of renewable fuel demand growth through 2030, with China, Brazil, Europe, India and the United States contributing more than two-thirds of global renewable fuel demand growth.
- Asia Pacific is expected to remain the fastest-growing biofuels market globally; per the IEA, India, Indonesia and China will account for a significant share of global biofuel demand growth through 2030.
- India policy stack cited as the demand driver: nationwide E20 petrol rollout, expansion of CBG and a phased SAF blending roadmap; India's ethanol production capacity exceeds 1,995 crore litres per annum (1,002 crore litres from grains and 992 crore litres from sugar derivatives).
- Europe: RED III requires either 29% renewable energy in transport or a 14.5% reduction in GHG intensity by 2030, including a 5.5% target for advanced biofuels and renewable fuels of non-biological origin; EU produced 16.8 billion litres of biodiesel, renewable diesel and SAF in 2024.
- United States: Renewable Fuel Standard continues to support ethanol, renewable diesel and SAF, with ~58 bn litres of ethanol produced annually and a SAF Grand Challenge target of 11 bn litres/year by 2030.
- Brazil: ethanol blending increased to E30 and biodiesel to B15 under the Fuel of the Future programme; Brazil is expected to account for nearly half (~40% per the policy table) of the global increase in biofuel demand through 2030.
- Indonesia: nationwide B40 biodiesel programme with discussions on progressing towards B50.
- Named growth drivers: energy security, net-zero commitments, feedstock diversification, Sustainable Aviation Fuel, and technology & innovation (advanced conversion technologies and commercialisation of second-generation biofuels).
- IEA World Energy Investment 2026 estimates global energy investment will reach a record US$3.4 trillion in 2026, with approximately US$2.2 trillion directed towards clean energy technologies, almost double the investment in fossil fuels.
- Risk noted within the outlook narrative: in North America 'policy uncertainty remains a potential risk'; Africa's development pace depends on investment in feedstock supply chains, infrastructure and enabling policy frameworks.

risks.note: The Board's Report states revenue 'was significantly impacted due to a sharp reduction in lifting by OMCs despite operational readiness and available production capacities'. This is a demand-side concentration risk the Company does not control: capacity and readiness were not the constraint, the buyer's lifting decision was. It is the single largest stated cause of the year's revenue shortfall.
risks.risk: Dependence on Oil Marketing Company offtake — OMCs sharply cut lifting despite the Company being production-ready

risks.note: The Board's Report attributes part of the revenue impact to 'delays in implementation and execution relating to the pending 15 crore litre allocation following the Hon'ble Karnataka High Court order'. Volumes the Company is counting on for recovery sit behind judicial and administrative execution rather than commercial demand, and the timing of realisation is outside management's control.
risks.risk: Unexecuted ethanol allocation contingent on a court order — the pending 15 crore litre allocation following the Hon'ble Karnataka High Court order

risks.note: The Board's Report states the fall in profit after tax was 'primarily attributable to an increase in finance costs arising from additional working capital facilities availed by the Company to support its business operations and also interest incurred on the account of grain-based plant established during the year', compounded by higher depreciation from capitalising the grain-based plant. Structurally: a capital-intensive expansion is being funded with debt while offtake is being withheld — the two risks compound. Credit standing is CRISIL A-/Stable (reaffirmed October 28, 2025) with India Ratings assigning IND A-/Stable / IND A2+ on bank loan facilities in April 2026.
risks.risk: Rising finance costs and leverage from the growth build-out

risks.note: A Secretarial Audit Report observation records that 'The Company failed to appoint the Woman Independent Director in compliance Regulation No. 17(1)a of SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015.' Management responds that the matter is receiving the highest priority and that it is in the advanced stage of finalizing a candidate, but the breach ran the full year in the Company's first year as a listed entity.
risks.risk: Governance compliance failure — no Woman Independent Director on the Board through the reporting period

risks.note: Listed by the Company as material issue 2 and classified as a pure Risk with NEGATIVE financial implications. Mitigation stated as advanced IT security systems, periodic vulnerability assessments and data encryption protocols. Relevant for an entity that has just become a listed, multi-site industrial operator with JV partners.

Material issues 4 and 5. Energy and Emissions Management is flagged as both Risk and Opportunity (positive and negative implications); Climate Strategy is flagged as a pure Risk with negative implications. For a biofuels producer this cuts both ways — the decarbonisation mandate is the demand driver, but the Company's own process emissions, feedstock footprint and carbon-intensity validation determine whether its product qualifies under tightening low-carbon fuel standards.

Material issue 12, a pure Risk with negative implications. The mitigation column concedes the Company 'is actively in the process of implementing a comprehensive Human Rights Policy' — i.e. the policy does not yet exist. The risks it names explicitly are forced labour, discrimination and unsafe working conditions, which is a live exposure given the Company's stated use of independent contractors overseeing on-site contract labour.
risks.risk: Human rights exposure with the governing policy not yet in place

risks.note: Material issue 13, a pure Risk with negative implications. The Company runs five distilleries plus five CBG plants under construction and a growing retail network; the Board's Report notes regular safety inspections and audits at 'all plants and project sites'. Construction-phase exposure is at its peak in FY27 with four CBG plants due for commissioning.
risks.risk: Employee health and safety across multi-site industrial and construction operations
